description: AstroCare es un equipo multicultural, unido por la pasión por la ciencia, la tecnología y la innovación. Con energía, creatividad y motivación, trabajamos para desarrollar una solución integral que permita monitorizar la salud física y mental de los astronautas durante las misiones espaciales. Creemos que la diversidad de perspectivas y el trabajo en equipo son la clave para superar los desafíos del futuro.
summary:
AstroCare is an interactive digital-health prototype designed to support astronaut health surveillance during long-duration space missions and explore the transfer of space-medicine approaches to remote healthcare on Earth.

Its objective is to bring physiological indicators, scheduled medical tests, laboratory and biometric records, and individual health trends into a single interface, helping users and medical teams review changes against personal baselines and identify information that may warrant further assessment.

The current prototype demonstrates a mobile-style monitoring interface with heart-rate and radiation indicators, configurable vital-sign tiles, medical-test scheduling, searchable dated records, trend charts, sample alerts, and an interactive body map. A complementary web dashboard presents a simulated crew health log, including longitudinal comparisons, measures grouped by body system, alert categories, and a measurement plan.

The chatbot, live wearable connectivity, and automated clinical support are planned extensions; they are not operational in the submitted prototype. Potential terrestrial applications include remote patient monitoring, telehealth, and health surveillance in geographically isolated or resource-limited settings.
details:
**The Human Body Beyond Earth**

AstroCare is a research-led digital health project combining a space medicine research framework with an interactive health-monitoring application.

The project brings together biomedical research on the physiological effects of long-duration spaceflight and a proposed technological solution for integrating, visualizing, and monitoring individual health information.

The current deliverable includes an informative website, an interactive mobile application prototype, and a complementary simulated crew health dashboard.

## 4. Project Details

### The Challenge

Long-duration human spaceflight exposes astronauts to physiological and environmental conditions that may affect multiple body systems. Research conducted aboard the International Space Station has identified relevant changes in blood physiology, bone density, radiation exposure, ocular structure, sleep, and circadian rhythms.

Monitoring these changes requires different types of assessments, including physiological measurements, laboratory analyses, imaging procedures, and specialized medical examinations.

The challenge is not simply collecting these measurements, but integrating them into a coherent health record that allows changes to be interpreted in relation to each astronaut's individual baseline and mission timeline.

AstroCare addresses this challenge by proposing an integrated digital platform for health monitoring and medical-test tracking during extended space missions.

### The Scientific Foundation

The AstroCare research framework is organized into five areas of astronaut health:

**1. Blood:** Changes in plasma volume, red blood cell mass, erythrocyte destruction, and hematological parameters.

**2. Bone:** Changes in bone mineral density, skeletal strength, and muscle-related indicators associated with microgravity.

**3. Radiation:** Cumulative radiation exposure, dosimetry, and the implications of deep-space radiation environments.

**4. Vision:** Ocular structural and refractive changes, including findings associated with Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

**5. Sleep:** Sleep duration, sleep disruption, insomnia indicators, and circadian rhythm alterations during spaceflight.

The research website presents the methods, findings, and conclusions of relevant human spaceflight studies, distinguishing published observations from estimates, interpolations, and projections for future deep-space missions.

### The Application

The current AstroCare prototype demonstrates an integrated mobile-style health-monitoring interface with six principal modules:

**1. Monitor**

Displays heart rate and daily radiation exposure, alongside configurable indicators such as blood oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep duration, exercise, and glucose.

**2. Medical Tests**

Provides a schedule of medical assessments, including blood sampling, ocular examinations using optical coherence tomography (OCT), sleep assessments, dosimeter checks, and bone density scans (DXA).

**3. Health Data and Records**

Organizes dated laboratory and biometric records, including blood chemistry, coagulation, vitamins, hormones, hydration, muscle and bone density, body mass, intraocular pressure, refractive changes, radiation exposure, and infection-related indicators.

Users can explore records through search and date filters.

**4. Trends**

Provides graphical representations of physiological measurements over time, allowing users to explore changes and compare available values with individual baseline measurements.

**5. Alerts**

Demonstrates a rule-based notification system that identifies predefined warnings and potentially relevant deviations in recorded measurements. Alerts can be reviewed and dismissed through the interface.

**6. Interactive Body Map**

Provides a rotatable anatomical schematic that connects body regions and physiological systems with their associated measurements and health information.

### The Web Dashboard

The complementary crew health dashboard demonstrates how longitudinal health information can be organized into a structured monitoring report.

Its functionalities include:

- Overview of individual health indicators.

- Visualization of physiological evolution over time.

- Comparisons between consecutive monitoring periods.

- Organization of measurements by body system.

- Identification and classification of sample alerts.

- Review of laboratory results and historical assessments.

- A structured measurement plan organized by monitoring frequency and operational priority.

The dashboard demonstrates how multiple health indicators can be brought together to provide a more comprehensive overview of an individual's physiological evolution throughout a mission.

### The AstroBand Concept

The project website also presents the AstroBand, a proposed lightweight, screen-free wearable designed to collect physiological measurements and transmit them to the AstroCare application through Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).

The conceptual design specifies a compact wristband, adjustable strap, extended battery life, and water resistance.

The wearable is intended to provide a continuous or periodic source of physiological information, reducing the need for astronauts to interact manually with monitoring equipment.

Physical hardware development and functional sensor connectivity remain future development steps.

### Future Applications

Although initially conceived for long-duration spaceflight, AstroCare has potential applications on Earth.

Its integrated monitoring architecture could be adapted to:

- Remote patient monitoring and telehealth.

- Longitudinal monitoring of individuals with chronic conditions.

- Healthcare provision in geographically isolated communities.

- Monitoring in expeditionary and other resource-limited environments.

- Digital health surveillance and preventive healthcare.

The broader objective is to translate technologies and monitoring approaches developed for space exploration into healthcare applications that may benefit populations on Earth.

## 5. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

The current prototype includes a dedicated AstroCare Assistant interface, designed to provide astronauts with an accessible way to interact with their health information.

The AI assistant is planned as a future development component. No operational AI model, external language-model API, speech recognition system, or scientific knowledge-base integration is present in the submitted application files.

The proposed AI architecture will connect a language model to a curated knowledge base of peer-reviewed biomedical literature and relevant space medicine research, potentially using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Its intended functionalities include:

- Retrieval and explanation of relevant scientific evidence.

- Contextualization of physiological measurements and laboratory results.

- Health education and preventive recommendations.

- Support for the initial assessment of acute health concerns.

- Identification of warning signs and guidance towards appropriate medical assessment or emergency protocols.

- Assistance with personalized health maintenance plans.

The assistant will be designed to provide source-referenced information, communicate uncertainty, and operate within clearly defined safety boundaries.

AI-generated information will complement clinical assessment rather than replace healthcare professionals or independently establish medical diagnoses.

## 6. NASA Data

NASA research constitutes a primary scientific foundation of AstroCare.

The project's research website and supporting dashboard draw on publicly available NASA human spaceflight research, technical reports, and biomedical investigations to identify physiological changes relevant to long-duration missions.

The NASA resources referenced in the current research framework include:

- **NASA Human Research Program:** research on health risks associated with human spaceflight.

- **NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO):** technical information on human health and medical requirements in space.

- **NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS):** published technical research and investigations.

- **NASA Space Radiation Analysis Group (SRAG):** information concerning astronaut radiation monitoring and dosimetry.

- **NASA-STD-3001:** human performance and health-related requirements for spaceflight.

Specific research topics incorporated into the project include:

- Spaceflight-associated changes in red blood cell destruction and blood physiology.

- Risk of spaceflight-induced bone changes.

- Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS).

- Radiation exposure and astronaut dosimetry.

- Sleep accommodations and circadian disruption during spaceflight.

The research framework also incorporates published NASA measurements and scientific estimates to explain physiological changes over time.

Where appropriate, the project distinguishes directly measured observations from interpolated trends and projections for future missions to Mars. These projections are not presented as established outcomes in human astronauts.

**Data integration status:** NASA research findings and scientific references inform the current project. However, the submitted prototype does not yet include direct programmatic integration of NASA datasets, live NASA data feeds, or automated downloads from NASA repositories.

## 7. Space Agency Partner & Other Data

### Space Agency Resources

NASA is the principal space agency referenced in the current AstroCare research framework. Its human spaceflight investigations, technical publications, and health-related research provide the scientific foundation for the selection of monitored parameters and the design of the proposed health-monitoring system.

NASA and NOAA

- NASA, The Human Body in Space: https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/the-human-body-in-space/

- NASA, Astronaut exercise research on the ISS: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/astronaut-exercise/

- NASA, Integrated Medical Model: https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasas-integrated-medical-model-imm/

Books and papers

- Gómez Ayala and Puente Durán, Enfermería espacial, 2018 (Agencia Espacial Mexicana)

- BMJ Open, NASA astronaut cohort profile: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/16/6/e112490

- NCBI Bookshelf, clinical guidelines: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK11822/

- PMC11640209, diagnosis and recommendations for vaginal microbiota diseases: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11640209/

Software and tools

- Apple HealthKit and WatchConnectivity (Swift, SwiftUI)

- Android Health Connect, ML Kit and CameraX (only if you show the Android app)

- Medi Assistent first-aid trainer (only if it is in the demo and not your own work; credit its authors)

Other Scientific and Biomedical Sources

In addition to NASA publications, AstroCare's research framework draws on peer-reviewed scientific literature and biomedical studies addressing the physiological effects of human spaceflight. The project aims to maintain a research-led approach in which scientific observations, individual measurements, and future projections are clearly distinguished. The references incorporated into the research website and supporting report include studies concerning:

- Red blood cell destruction and hematological changes during spaceflight.

- Bone density, skeletal strength, and muscle deconditioning.

- Ocular structural changes and SANS.

- Radiation measurements during human spaceflight and deep-space exploration.

- Sleep duration, insomnia, and circadian disruption.

These publications provide the evidence base for identifying relevant physiological indicators, organizing the project's health-monitoring framework, and contextualizing the information presented in the demonstrator.
